global.headline: THE IAEA REFERS IRAN TO THE SECURITY COUNCIL FOR THE FIRST TIME IN TWENTY YEARS — AND OIL CROSSES US$100 ON THE SAME DAY THE US SINKS FIVE TANKERS AND IRAN FIRES ON JORDAN
summary: The International Atomic Energy Agency's 35-member Board of Governors voted on Wednesday to refer Iran to the United Nations Security Council over non-compliance with its nuclear safeguards obligations — 23 votes in favour, three against, eight abstentions and one member not voting, with Russia, China and Niger opposed. The resolution was submitted by Britain, France, Germany and the United States. It is the first such referral of Iran in twenty years, and it lands on a file the agency has been unable to inspect: the IAEA has had no access to Iran's declared enrichment sites since the June 2025 strikes, and 440.9kg of uranium enriched to 60 per cent was last physically observed there.

Iran's response was to attack the premise rather than the finding. Reza Najafi, Tehran's ambassador in Vienna, called the resolution a "political tool" that had ruined confidence in the agency's "independence, impartiality and credibility" and was "completely counterproductive", and said that American and Israeli airstrikes had made safe access for inspectors "materially impossible" — Iran had "neither stopped nor suspended its safeguards obligations", but "performance is currently impossible under continuing military operations and persistent threats". Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi put the circularity more sharply on X: "They attack Iran's safeguarded nuclear facilities, disrupt the normal verification process, and then use that very disruption as a pretext for passing a resolution at the IAEA Board of Governors." The Security Council the file has now been sent to contains two of the three states that voted against sending it, both holding vetoes.

Underneath the diplomacy, the exchange rate of the war moved again. CENTCOM struck five Iranian crude carriers — the M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, M/T Riesco and M/T Derya, four in the Gulf of Oman and one near Kharg Island — sinking at least one, after the IRGC tried twice in two days to hit a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles. This is the third and largest application of the tanker-for-tanker formula Adm. Brad Cooper published on 6 September. Iran answered overnight with more than 20 ballistic missiles at Jordan's Muwaffaq Salti air base near Azraq, the principal host of US air operations in the kingdom; the Jordanian army said its defences engaged 20 and destroyed 18, with the remainder falling in unpopulated areas. The IRGC claimed heavy damage to F-35, F-16 and F-15 maintenance and shelter facilities; US officials said the damage was limited. CENTCOM then struck Iranian air-defence systems, command centres and drone and rocket launch sites in response.

Separately, CSIS analysts reviewing six years of satellite imagery reported a surge of construction this year at Pickaxe Mountain, the granite-covered site near the Natanz complex about 225km south of Tehran that intelligence agencies regard as the likely home of a protected future Iranian enrichment programme. The work has shifted from excavation toward internal construction and exterior hardening — raised and reinforced tunnel portals, a paved internal road network, more road activity than in any prior year — while Washington is publicly weighing how to strike targets that deep. The analysts' own caution is the important part: continuous construction suggests the site is not yet capable of enrichment.

Brent crude rose nearly 3 per cent to US$100.72 (roughly S$129) a barrel on Wednesday, its first move above US$100 since July, and US benchmark WTI gained 2.4 per cent to US$95.25 (roughly S$122); CNN put the intraday peak at US$101. American diesel hit a record US$5.94 (about S$7.60) a gallon. Trump, speaking to reporters on his way to the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, said he expects Iran to abandon the war "immediately after the election" — arguing Tehran is near collapse and is prolonging the fight into November to damage him politically — and conceded that pump prices would not fall before then, and that his promised sub-US$2 gasoline would "take a little bit longer than the midterm".
global.geopolitical: The referral is historically weighty and practically hollow, and both halves matter. For the first time since 2006 the nuclear file has been moved out of the technical body and into the political one — but it arrives at a Council where Russia and China, who voted against sending it, can stop anything that follows. What the vote does accomplish is to put the E3 formally alongside Washington on the nuclear question at the exact moment those same three states are breaking with it on Israel, which complicates any Iranian read of Europe as an available counterweight. Tehran's argument is also stronger than a censure vote allows for: the agency cannot verify what it cannot visit, and it cannot visit sites that are being bombed. That leaves a settlement, whenever one is attempted, with no agreed baseline for the 440.9kg stockpile — and the Pickaxe Mountain imagery suggests Iran is building toward a programme that would be harder to inspect and harder to hit even if one existed. Meanwhile the kinetic war has settled into a legible pattern with an illegible endpoint: missiles at American warships answered by strikes on the tanker fleet that funds the IRGC, answered in turn by missiles at a third country's air base. Jordan has now absorbed several rounds of fire aimed at the Americans it hosts, without becoming a combatant. Trump's framing — that the war ends on his electoral calendar rather than on any negotiated one — is a statement about domestic politics offered as a forecast of Iranian behaviour, and it is the closest thing to a stated endpoint the administration has given in weeks.
global.socioeconomic: The US$100 barrel is the number that reaches households, and it now has two independent drivers: Iranian interference with Hormuz, and Houthi fire on Saudi facilities and Red Sea shipping. Brent at US$100.72 (roughly S$129) is about 40 per cent above where it sat before the summer's escalation, and the American diesel record of US$5.94 (about S$7.60) a gallon is the more consequential figure, because diesel prices propagate through freight, agriculture and construction rather than through commuting alone. For Singapore, an entrepôt that refines and bunkers what it does not consume, the transmission runs through fuel costs, electricity tariffs and shipping rates rather than through supply — the Q3 tariff already sits at a record 34.78 cents/kWh with GST. Trump's own accounting is the striking part: he conceded pump prices will stay elevated for at least the eight weeks to the midterms, which concedes that the war's cost is being carried by American consumers in the interim and that the administration has no near-term instrument to change that. Sinking five tankers removes revenue from the IRGC and simultaneously removes barrels from a market that is already short of them; the campaign's economic logic and its price consequences point in opposite directions.

global.headline: SAUDI ARABIA BOMBS YEMEN FOR THE FIRST TIME IN FOUR YEARS — 32 STRIKES IN A DAY — AND ITS OWN CRUDE EXPORTS FALL TO A NINE-YEAR LOW AS BOTH ESCAPE ROUTES CLOSE
summary: Houthi media reported 32 Saudi airstrikes across Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeidah on Wednesday — the clearest sign yet that Riyadh has resumed the air campaign it formally suspended four years ago, and the answer to the question this pipeline has been carrying since July over whether Saudi Arabia moves from host of American operations to declared party. It follows Tuesday's Houthi barrage on Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, which wounded 73 civilians and set fires at energy installations, and weeks of Houthi ground offensives around Taiz, Marib, Hodeidah and al-Dhale that have already displaced civilians and, on one accounting, killed at least 129 in the Taiz fighting alone. Houthi shelling of a displaced-persons camp in Marib killed two children and injured 15.

The economic consequence arrived in the same window. Observed Saudi crude exports have fallen to roughly 3 million barrels a day, the lowest in at least nine years, according to tanker-tracking data — not because the kingdom cannot produce, but because it is running out of ways to ship. Iran's restriction of Hormuz pushed Aramco's barrels west to the Red Sea terminal at Yanbu; the Houthi threat in the Red Sea is now pushing them back east to Gulf terminals, or all the way around Africa, adding thousands of miles per voyage. Two tankers carrying Saudi crude were hit by projectiles in the strait this week; one was owned by the state shipping arm Bahri, which said two seafarers were killed.

This is the front reopened on 14 July, when Yemen's Riyadh-backed government struck Sanaa airport's runway and the Houthis retaliated on Abha, ending a four-year truce. Since then it has produced a declared maritime embargo on Saudi-bound shipping (20 July), strikes on the tankers Encelia and Layla (23 July), three separate hits on the Jizan refining complex in two months, and now a resumed Saudi air campaign. What began as a proxy adjunct to the Iran war has become a second war with its own escalation ladder.
global.geopolitical: Four years of Saudi restraint in Yemen has ended, and it ended without a formal announcement — 32 strikes in a day is the announcement. Riyadh's calculation had been that absorbing Houthi fire was cheaper than re-entering a war it could not win and had spent years extricating itself from; Tuesday's 73 wounded civilians and the fires at its energy installations appear to have changed that arithmetic. The danger is that the kingdom is now fighting a movement that is supplied by, but not commanded by, Tehran, which means a Hormuz settlement between Washington and Iran would not end this front. It also means the Gulf's most important American partner is now a belligerent in two overlapping conflicts simultaneously, at a moment when its own defensive capacity is being tested by drones and ballistic missiles rather than by aircraft. For Yemen itself, the resumption of coalition air power over Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeidah returns a country with the world's worst humanitarian indicators to full-scale war after four years of a truce that, whatever its failures, had stopped the bombing.
global.socioeconomic: Saudi crude exports at a nine-year low of roughly 3 million barrels a day is the single most important supply number in the current oil market, and it is not a production decision — it is a shipping one. The kingdom built the East-West pipeline to Yanbu precisely to escape Hormuz; the Houthis have now made the escape route as dangerous as the thing it escapes, and Aramco is left choosing between two threatened chokepoints or a circumnavigation of Africa that adds weeks and cost to every cargo. This is why Brent crossed US$100 (roughly S$129) this week on Yemen rather than on Iran: the market has priced Iranian disruption for months, but Saudi barrels were the assumed cushion. Two dead Bahri seafarers is the other cost, and it belongs alongside the 20 seafarers and one port worker already killed in the strait since 28 February — the people absorbing this war are increasingly merchant crews on ships flying flags with no stake in it. For importers such as Singapore, the durable lesson is that bypass infrastructure built to route around one chokepoint is only as good as the security of the second one.

global.headline: THE FBI, NSA AND CISA ACCUSE CHINESE AI FIRMS OF "INDUSTRIAL-SCALE" THEFT FROM AMERICAN MODELS, NAMING ALIBABA AND DEEPSEEK — AND BEIJING CALLS IT GROUNDLESS
summary: A joint advisory from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the National Security Agency and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency alleges that Chinese artificial-intelligence companies are conducting "industrial-scale" theft of American competitors' trade secrets in order to cut development costs and reach market faster. The named technique is distillation — querying a frontier model at volume in order to "extract restricted proprietary functionalities and capabilities", then training on the outputs. The advisory names Alibaba Group and DeepSeek among firms it says ran "high-volume knowledge distillation campaigns" against US counterparts, and describes a grey market of proxies known as "transfer stations" used to evade the geographic restrictions, safeguards and terms of use that American labs apply.

The most concrete figure comes from Anthropic, which alleges that three Chinese AI laboratories generated more than 16 million exchanges with its Claude models through roughly 24,000 fraudulent accounts. Separately, the company disclosed a fourth AI-enabled hacking incident that its earlier review had missed.

China's foreign ministry rejected the advisory outright. Spokesperson Mao Ning said Chinese AI development reflects the country's high level of self-reliance and its strength in science and technology, and that the United States should refrain from "unfounded accusations against or smearing China".
global.geopolitical: This is the first time the American security agencies have described competition between AI laboratories in the vocabulary they normally reserve for state-sponsored espionage, and the shift in framing is the story. Distillation is not intrusion: it uses a model's public interface as designed, at scale, through intermediaries — which means the alleged conduct sits in the gap between commercial terms-of-service violation and national-security offence, and the advisory is an attempt to move it decisively into the second category. That matters for what follows, because export controls can restrict chips but cannot restrict queries, and there is no established instrument for policing what a foreign competitor learns from talking to your model. Naming Alibaba and DeepSeek specifically also converts a diffuse concern into a list, which is how sanctions regimes usually begin. The timing is pointed: Washington is pressing Southeast Asia to commit to Pax Silica, its bid for a China-free AI supply chain, while Beijing recruits the same governments into its own AI organisation. An advisory that casts Chinese frontier labs as thieves is, among other things, an argument aimed at the governments now choosing between the two blocs.
global.socioeconomic: If the allegation holds, the economics of frontier AI are less defensible than the capital being poured into them assumes: the cost asymmetry between spending billions to train a model and spending a fraction of that to distil its capabilities through 24,000 fraudulent accounts is the kind of gap that changes who can profitably build one. That threatens the basic investment case for very large training runs, since the returns depend on the resulting capability staying proprietary long enough to earn back the compute. The practical consequence for users will be friction — stricter identity verification, rate limits, regional blocks and higher barriers to API access, applied to everyone in order to catch a few. For countries with AI ambitions but no frontier laboratories of their own, Singapore included, the risk is that both blocs harden their terms of access at once, and that being a customer of American models starts to carry conditions about who else you may work with.

global.headline: WASHINGTON BANS CANADIAN ALCOHOL, DAIRY AND MOTORCYCLES OUTRIGHT — MOVING FROM TARIFFS TO PROHIBITION AS OTTAWA'S COUNTER-TARIFFS TAKE HOLD
summary: The United States has imposed outright import bans on a list of Canadian goods, published on the White House website and taking effect on 29 September, hours after Canada's retaliatory tariffs on roughly US$20 billion (about S$26 billion) of American goods came into force. The bans appear to cover most alcohol — beer, wine, whisky, bourbon, rum, vodka, vermouth, tequila, mezcal and brandy — along with whey protein, invert molasses, cane molasses and non-alcoholic beer, plus motorcycles. Various cheese products were not banned but were added to a list carrying a 50 per cent tariff.

The distinction matters more than the product list. A tariff prices a good out of a market and leaves the buyer a choice; a prohibition removes the transaction entirely, and there is no rate at which a Canadian distiller can compete. Trump separately threatened on Truth Social to block Bombardier's sales in the United States unless the Montreal manufacturer builds its aircraft in America — "their products aren't good enough" — drawing pushback from at least one Republican senator and knocking the company's shares.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has suspended talks over what he called unfair terms and has been arguing that Canada must reorient its economy away from the United States. The two countries conduct one of the largest bilateral trading relationships in the world, and roughly three-quarters of Canadian exports go south.
global.geopolitical: The move from tariffs to bans is a categorical change, not an incremental one, and it is being applied to a treaty ally inside an existing free-trade agreement. Tariffs, however punitive, still operate within the logic of trade; an import prohibition is the instrument states normally reserve for sanctioned adversaries or genuine safety hazards, and using it on Canadian whisky and motorcycles empties the agreement of meaning while it is still nominally in force. The Bombardier threat makes the underlying demand explicit — manufacture in the United States or lose access to it — which is industrial relocation pursued through market exclusion. For Carney the political effect is to make his reorientation argument for him, though the arithmetic of that reorientation remains brutal given how much of Canada's economy points at a single customer. The wider signal reaches every country with an American trade agreement, Singapore included: the agreement is not the ceiling on what can be done to you, and the escalation ladder now has a rung above tariffs.
global.socioeconomic: Canadian distillers, brewers, dairy processors and motorcycle manufacturers lose their largest market on 29 September with no tariff-shaped workaround, and the affected sectors are concentrated in specific provinces rather than spread across the economy — meaning the damage will land as regional shocks rather than as a diffuse drag. American consumers lose the products; American importers, distributors and retailers lose the margin, which is why the pushback on Bombardier came from within the president's own party. The 50 per cent tariff on cheese is the more instructive line item, since it shows the administration deliberately choosing between pricing and prohibition product by product. For third countries the immediate effect is displaced supply looking for new buyers, and the longer-term effect is a risk premium on any supply chain whose final destination is the United States — a calculation Singapore's own exporters and the region's transshipment hubs are already making as Washington presses its "transshipment" case across Southeast Asia.

global.headline: MERZ CANCELS HIS CALL WITH TRUMP AFTER THE PRESIDENT CELEBRATES THE AfD'S RECORD WIN — THEN ACCUSES THE PARTY OF "ETHNIC CLEANSING" IN THE BUNDESTAG
summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz cancelled a scheduled telephone call with President Trump after Trump posted on Truth Social celebrating the far-right AfD's result in Saxony-Anhalt: "Wow, the populist party in Germany had a really big night", signed off "MGGA!!!" Government spokesman Stefan Kornelius confirmed Berlin had requested the postponement and said no new date had been set; the spokesman declined to give a reason, though Merz has said repeatedly that foreign "interference or comments regarding the domestic political situation in Germany, especially in connection with elections" are unacceptable to him.

Merz then went to the Bundestag and attacked the party directly, clashing with AfD leader Alice Weidel and accusing the AfD of pursuing a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" of skilled workers. He has conceded that the Saxony-Anhalt result — 43.8 per cent and 39 of 83 seats, three short of a majority — shook his CDU "to its very foundations".
The AfD's route to governing the state runs through the BSW, which cleared the 5 per cent threshold and enters the Landtag as kingmaker. Merz faces two further state elections this month.
global.geopolitical: A German chancellor refusing to take an American president's call is a small act with an unusually clear meaning: Berlin has decided that being seen to accept the endorsement is more costly than the rupture of not talking. The Brandmauer — the cross-party refusal to govern with or through the AfD — has held at every level of German politics precisely because it was a domestic consensus that no external actor tried to break; an American president publicly cheering the party turns the firewall into a transatlantic dispute, which is exactly the framing the AfD wants and the CDU cannot afford. Merz's problem is that his own answer is rhetorical escalation in the Bundestag while the arithmetic in Magdeburg stays unchanged, and the party three seats from a majority now needs only the BSW, which shares little of the AfD's programme but much of its position on Russia and Ukraine. That combination — a state government resting on two parties sympathetic to Moscow — would have consequences well beyond Saxony-Anhalt, at a moment when Washington's envoys are working a Ukraine settlement and European unity on Russia is the main thing Kyiv still has.
global.socioeconomic: Merz's "ethnic cleansing" charge is aimed at a real economic exposure rather than only at the AfD's rhetoric: Germany's manufacturing base and its care and health systems depend on skilled migration to offset a demographic decline that domestic births will not close, and a governing party committed to reversing that flow would be constraining labour supply in the sectors already shortest of it. Businesses have been unusually direct about this, because recruitment decisions are made years ahead and political risk of this kind shows up first as skilled workers choosing another country. The immediate cost is uncertainty in an economy that has had little growth to spare, and the transatlantic component compounds it — Berlin is managing a trade relationship with Washington while declining the president's calls. For Singaporean firms with German operations, and for the German companies that use Singapore as their Southeast Asian base, the relevant question is not who governs Saxony-Anhalt but whether Germany's migration settlement, on which its industrial capacity rests, is now genuinely in play.

singapore.headline: ISD SAYS THE TERROR THREAT REMAINS HIGH AND THE RADICALISED ARE GETTING YOUNGER — SIX YOUTH CASES IN A YEAR, THREE OF THEM FOURTEEN-YEAR-OLDS
summary: The Internal Security Department's Singapore Terrorism Threat Assessment Report, released early Thursday, keeps the threat level at high, with no specific intelligence of an imminent attack. ISD attributes the elevated level in part to the Middle East conflicts, which terrorist and extremist groups are exploiting for their own agendas — three of the eight Singaporeans dealt with under the Internal Security Act between July 2025 and this year were radicalised by the re-escalation of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict from October 2023.

The sharpest finding is about age. Youth ISA cases have risen from four in the five years to 2021 to 15 in the five years to 2026, with six identified in the past year alone: three 14-year-olds, one 15-year-old and two 19-year-olds. Three of those detained between April and June this year, aged 14 to 19, had formulated local attack plans and were close to executing them. Of the 23 youths dealt with under the ISA over the past decade, more than half had intended to launch attacks in Singapore, having identified weapons and researched bomb-making before arrest. The youngest person ever detained under the Act is now 14.

Self-radicalisation remains the dominant pathway — seven of the eight Singaporeans dealt with under the ISA in the past year were self-radicalised, overwhelmingly online rather than through any organised local network. Since 2022, 156 Singaporeans have been issued ISA orders: 106 detentions and 50 restriction orders, with 87 of the detained since released.
singapore.geopolitical: The report makes explicit a link Singapore has generally handled carefully — that a war fought thousands of kilometres away radicalises people here, and that the strait, the sanctions and the oil price are not the only channels through which the Middle East reaches this country. That is an uncomfortable position for a state whose foreign policy rests on non-alignment and on being useful to everyone: neutrality abroad does not produce neutrality in how citizens experience the conflict, and the six women charged this week over unpermitted pro-Palestinian assemblies sit on the same continuum, at its lawful end. The release date is also worth noting, arriving the day before the 25th anniversary of 11 September and in the same week ISD is arguing for continued vigilance. The durable point is that the ISA caseload is no longer about networks or returning fighters but about individuals radicalising alone on their phones — a threat model that intelligence work is structurally poor at detecting, since there is no organisation to penetrate.
singapore.socioeconomic: Three 14-year-olds in a single year moves this from a security problem to a schools-and-families problem, and it is worth being precise about what the numbers show: the cases are not clustered in any one community institution but in the unsupervised online space that every teenager in Singapore occupies. The 87 releases from 106 detentions is the other half of the story and the part most easily missed — the rehabilitation programme is doing most of the work, and it is measured over years of religious counselling and family engagement rather than in arrests. The cost falls on teachers, parents and counsellors asked to notice a change in a child before the state does, which is a real burden being placed on people with no training for it. It also sharpens the practical question raised elsewhere in Parliament this week about young people using AI chatbots for religious answers: the same device that provides the radicalising material is now also the first place a curious 14-year-old goes for an authoritative-sounding response.

singapore.headline: PARLIAMENT PASSES THE SCAMS BILL: SELLING YOUR SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT NOW CARRIES JAIL AND THE CANE, AND PLATFORM FINES RISE TENFOLD TO S$10 MILLION
summary: The Scams (Countermeasures) and Other Matters Bill passed on Wednesday, creating a new offence of acting as an online account mule. It is now an offence to supply personal details for the creation of such accounts, and to supply or buy the accounts themselves for criminal use — on platforms including Carousell, TikTok, Telegram and Meta's services. Convicted online account mules face up to three years' jail, a fine of up to S$10,000 and up to 12 strokes of the cane.

The maximum fine for online service providers that fail to comply with codes of practice or implementation directives rises from S$1 million to S$10 million. The providers currently within scope include WhatsApp, Telegram, WeChat, Apple, Google, Carousell, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok. The Bill also widens police powers to disable accounts suspected of facilitating scams and to restrict services used in them.

Minister of State Goh Pei Ming addressed the obvious objection during the debate: account holders restricted for suspected mule activity will not be cut off from money for daily expenses. The framing throughout was that Singapore has spent years pursuing money mules and is now extending the same logic upstream, to the identities and accounts that scams are run through before any money moves.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is again legislating ahead of the jurisdictions that host the platforms, and the tenfold increase in the maximum fine is calibrated to a specific problem: S$1 million is not a deterrent to companies of this size, and S$10 million is closer to being one. The regulatory model on display — name the platforms, issue codes of practice, attach a fine large enough to be noticed, and take the power to act on accounts directly — is one that other small, highly-online states have copied from Singapore before, and it will be read in the region as a template. The friction to watch is jurisdictional: the offences and the account-disabling powers apply to conduct here, while the accounts, the servers and the syndicates mostly sit elsewhere, which is why the Bill leans on compelling platform cooperation rather than on pursuing the operators. It also extends the state's reach into private accounts on foreign platforms, which is a meaningful expansion however narrowly it is drawn.
singapore.socioeconomic: The new offence targets a genuinely low-status, low-paid link in the scam chain — people who sell a verified account for a few hundred dollars, often young, often in debt, frequently unaware that it will be used for fraud — and it answers that with jail and caning. The deterrent logic is that syndicates cannot function without a steady supply of clean local identities, so raising the cost of supplying one raises the cost of the whole operation; the risk is that the people caught are the most replaceable and least culpable participants, while the organisers remain offshore and untouched. Goh's assurance on daily expenses matters practically: an account restriction can otherwise leave someone unable to pay rent or buy food while an investigation runs. For platform operators the S$10 million exposure changes the internal economics of compliance in Singapore, and compliance teams tend to be built once and applied regionally, so the effect may reach well beyond the users this Parliament represents.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE IS WEIGHING AN INVITATION TO JOIN CHINA'S AI ORGANISATION WHILE WASHINGTON PRESSES THE REGION INTO A CHINA-FREE SUPPLY CHAIN
summary: Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo told Parliament on Wednesday that Singapore "will consider the invitation alongside our broader engagements with China and other international AI cooperation initiatives" — the invitation being membership of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation, the body China proposed and formally established on 16 July with 29 founding signatories and a headquarters in Shanghai, oriented toward the Global South.

Five ASEAN states are already founding members: Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia and Myanmar. On the other side, Washington wants the region committed to Pax Silica, its effort to build an artificial-intelligence supply chain that excludes China. Both capitals have been pressing Southeast Asian governments to choose since at least late August.

The reply Teo gave is the careful one — considering, not declining, and explicitly placed within a wider set of engagements rather than treated as a choice of camp. It landed in the same 24 hours as an American security advisory accusing Chinese laboratories of industrial-scale theft from US models.
singapore.geopolitical: This is the AI-era version of the position Singapore has held on every other axis of US-China competition, and it is getting harder to hold rather than easier. WAICO is designed as an institution rather than an initiative — a headquarters, a membership, a Global South orientation — which means joining is a durable commitment rather than a gesture, and declining is a legible refusal. Five ASEAN members have already signed, so non-alignment no longer means moving with the bloc; the bloc has split. Teo's formulation buys time by treating the invitation as one item in a portfolio of engagements, but the American advisory published in the same window is precisely the kind of event designed to make the portfolio framing untenable, by recasting membership as association with conduct Washington calls theft. Singapore's structural interest is unchanged: it hosts the data centres, the regional headquarters and the chips, and it needs both the American models and the Chinese market. The question is whether a position that requires both sides to tolerate ambiguity survives a period in which neither is inclined to.
singapore.socioeconomic: Singapore's AI ambitions are downstream of hardware it does not make and models it does not train, which is exactly why bloc membership is an economic question and not only a diplomatic one. Access to advanced chips runs through American export-control decisions; access to the region's largest market and to a rapidly improving set of Chinese open-weight models runs through Beijing. A commitment that narrows either would have direct consequences for the data-centre investment, the regional AI headquarters and the enterprise deployments that Singapore has spent years attracting — and the country's own national AI programmes assume continued access to both stacks. The near-term risk is not exclusion but conditionality: terms of access from either side that require choices about the other, applied to firms operating here. That is the quiet cost of the bloc competition for a country whose entire economic model is built on being the place where both sides are comfortable doing business.

singapore.headline: CAT A COE CROSSES S$130,000 FOR THE FIRST TIME, CLOSING AT A RECORD S$133,009, WITH ALL FIVE CATEGORIES UP
summary: Premiums rose across the board in the first September bidding exercise, which closed at 4pm on Wednesday. Category A — cars up to 1,600cc and 97kW — gained 3.51 per cent to close at a record S$133,009, crossing S$130,000 for the first time and beating the previous high of S$129,000 set on 8 July by S$4,009. It is the second record for the category this year.

Category B closed at S$135,001, Category C at S$93,101, Category D at S$12,556 and Category E at S$137,890. OneMotoring recorded 4,776 bids against a quota of 3,253, with 1,152 successful bids in Category A, 910 in B, 306 in C, 495 in D and 300 in E.
The Land Transport Authority attributed the elevated prices in part to the three-week gap since the previous exercise, and urged buyers and dealers to be prudent in bidding.
singapore.geopolitical: Little directly, but the COE is the clearest domestic instrument through which Singapore's external conditions become a household number. The quota is set by deregistrations and by the government's zero-growth vehicle policy rather than by demand, so when demand is firm the price absorbs everything — including a fuel-cost environment set by a war in the Gulf and a general-price environment shaped by the same disruption. That the LTA felt the need to urge prudence, twice-yearly records notwithstanding, points at the political sensitivity of a system in which the state sets the supply and then asks buyers to restrain themselves against it. The policy question that will not go away is whether a mechanism designed to ration road space should be producing a certificate that costs more than most of the cars it is attached to.
singapore.socioeconomic: S$133,009 for the right to put a small car on the road for ten years, before the car itself, is the number, and it works out to roughly S$1,108 a month in certificate cost alone. The immediate effect falls on the businesses and families for whom a car is not discretionary — and Category C at S$93,101 for goods vehicles feeds directly into delivery and trade costs at a moment when diesel is at record levels globally. The three-week gap the LTA cited explains the timing of the spike but not its level: the underlying pressure is a small quota against sustained demand, with buyers who have seen the price rise for long enough to expect it to keep rising, which is itself a reason to bid now. Against Q3 electricity at a record 34.78 cents/kWh with GST and transport inflation already running well above the headline rate, this is the second large fixed cost of getting around Singapore to set a record this quarter.

singapore.headline: KHAW BOON WAN STEPS DOWN AT SPH MEDIA TRUST AFTER FIVE YEARS, WITH CEO CHAN YENG KIT TAKING THE CHAIR AS WELL
summary: SPH Media Trust chairman Khaw Boon Wan will step down on 1 October after five years, with chief executive Chan Yeng Kit taking on the chairmanship while remaining CEO. The changes were agreed after consultation with SMT's institutional members and board directors and remain subject to regulatory approval.

Khaw, 73, a former Cabinet minister who held the health, national development and transport portfolios before retiring from politics in 2020, framed the exit in plain terms: "As the SPH operations have stabilised, I think it is a good time for me, a retiree, to wind down my involvement in this project." He took the chairmanship in 2021 when the company's media business was restructured into a not-for-profit entity backed by public funding, and steered it through the circulation-data overstatement episode that followed.

In parallel remarks he said the role had given him a better appreciation of the pressures on newsrooms and journalists — a notable line from a former minister who spent his political career on the other side of that relationship.
singapore.geopolitical: Nothing external, but the governance question is real: combining the chair and the chief executive at the company that publishes The Straits Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu concentrates two roles that are separated precisely so one can check the other. SMT is not an ordinary company — it was restructured as a not-for-profit with public funding attached, on the argument that national news provision is a public good that the commercial model could no longer sustain — which makes the board's independence from management the principal safeguard the public has. The consolidation may well be temporary and pragmatic, and it requires regulatory approval, but it deserves to be named rather than passed over. Khaw's own remark about better appreciating what newsrooms face is the more interesting note, and it is the kind of thing more easily said on the way out than on the way in.
singapore.socioeconomic: Khaw arrived to stabilise a business that had been losing money and readers, and inherited within months a scandal over overstated circulation figures; "operations have stabilised" is a modest way to describe finishing that job. What has not changed is the underlying economics that produced the restructuring — advertising has gone to platforms, subscription revenue does not replace it, and the funding gap is now met publicly, which converts a commercial problem into a recurring fiscal one and ties the newsroom's independence to a subsidy that must be periodically justified. Chan, a former permanent secretary at the Ministry of Health, takes on both roles at a point when the harder question is not stabilisation but what a public-funded national news organisation is for over the next decade, in a market where a growing share of readers get their news from platforms this same Parliament is currently legislating fines for.

word.definition: Of no real value or effect; futile, trifling, inoperative. The word does two jobs at once, and the second is the useful one: it describes something that is not merely small but formally void — an action correctly performed that nonetheless produces nothing. A clause can be nugatory, and so can a vote, a warning or a treaty.
word.etymology: From Latin nūgātōrius, 'worthless, trifling', from nūgārī, 'to trifle or jest', from nūgae, 'jokes, trifles, nonsense'. It entered English in the early seventeenth century and settled quickly into legal and diplomatic use, where the need to say that a properly executed instrument has no operative effect comes up more often than one would hope. The buried image is of an argument made in jest — something offered with the form of seriousness and none of the substance.
word.example: The IAEA board's referral of Iran to the Security Council on Wednesday was historic and, in almost the same breath, nugatory: the first such vote in twenty years, carried 23 to three, and sent to a body where two of the three states that opposed it hold vetoes.
